The last 15 questions are three passage sets (factual, narrative, literary) of 5 questions each; each set stays together.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
After the national anthem, the chief guest will ________ to the stage to light the lamp.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) proceed
Why: "Proceed" means to move forward or go on to a place or action.
Why not the others: (A) "Precede" means to come before. (C) means to move back. (D) means to replace.
Key point: Pro- means forward; pre- means before.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The doctor asked the patient to ________ deeply.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) breathe
Why: After "to", a verb is needed; "breathe" (with -e) is the verb.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) are the noun. (C) means width.
Key point: Breath is the noun; breathe is the verb.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The shop sells a wide ________ of spices from Kerala.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) variety
Why: After "a wide", a noun is needed: "a wide variety of".
Why not the others: (A) is an adjective. (B) is a verb. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: A wide variety of, a wide range of.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Only students who have passed Class 12 are ________ to apply.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) eligible
Why: "Eligible" means having the right qualifications to do something.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) describe handwriting that cannot or can be read. (C) means not qualified, the opposite.
Key point: Eligible for a post; legible handwriting.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to PERNICIOUS:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Harmful
Why: Pernicious means having a harmful effect, especially gradually or secretly.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) only look or sound similar.
Key point: Rumours can have a pernicious effect on a community.

questions.sub_topic: Antonym pairs: modest, exterior, hinder, major
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of antonyms:
A. modest — boastful
B. exterior — interior
C. hinder — obstruct
D. major — minor
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: B) B, C and D only
C) A, B, C and D
D) A, B and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A, B and D only
Why: Modest and boastful, exterior and interior, major and minor are opposites.
Why not the others: Pair C is a pair of synonyms — hinder means obstruct. Options (A), (B) and (C) include pair C.
Key point: Test each pair on its own.

questions.question:
Match the nouns in List-I with the verbs in List-II that they usually go with:

List-I
(A) ____ a complaint
(B) ____ a balance between work and rest
(C) Their efforts finally ____ fruit
(D) ____ a question at the meeting

List-II
(I) strike
(II) raise
(III) bear
(IV) lodge
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: Lodge a complaint (IV), strike a balance (I), efforts bear fruit (III), raise a question (II) are fixed collocations.
Why not the others: (A) gives "strike a complaint"; (B) gives "bear a balance"; (D) gives "raise fruit" in the wrong sense and "bear a question".
Key point: Collocations are learnt as pairs.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
It took her a month to ________ the fever.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) get over
Why: "Get over" means to recover from an illness or a shock.
Why not the others: (A) means to manage with little. (B) means to make progress or have a good relationship. (D) means to escape.
Key point: Get over an illness; get by on a small salary.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
The ________ boy hid his sister's shoes before school.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) mischievous
Why: The correct spelling is m-i-s-c-h-i-e-v-o-u-s, with no "i" before "-ous".
Why not the others: (A) adds an extra "i". (C) misses the "i" after "h". (D) reverses "ie" to "ei".
Key point: Mischievous has three syllables, not four.

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: dark horse, white elephant, red-letter day, add fuel to the fire
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) A dark horse
(B) A white elephant
(C) A red-letter day
(D) To add fuel to the fire

List-II
(I) A costly possession that is more trouble than it is worth
(II) A day of special importance or happiness
(III) To make a bad situation worse
(IV) A little-known person who unexpectedly succeeds
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: A dark horse — an unexpected winner (IV); a white elephant — a costly, useless possession (I); a red-letter day — a special day (II); add fuel to the fire — make things worse (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (B) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Colours in idioms do not have fixed meanings; learn each whole.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Fall out
(B) Fall through
(C) Fall back on
(D) Fall behind

List-II
(I) Quarrel
(II) Fail to happen
(III) Turn to for support when other things fail
(IV) Fail to keep up
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Friends fall out — quarrel (I); a plan falls through — fails (II); fall back on savings — rely on them (III); fall behind in studies — fail to keep up (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: The particle changes the meaning of "fall".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
Did she write this poem?
options: A) Was this poem written by her?
B) Is this poem written by her?
C) Has this poem been written by her?
D) Did this poem written by her?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Was this poem written by her?
Why: The simple past question "Did she write" becomes "Was ... written" in the passive.
Why not the others: (B) is in the present. (C) is in the present perfect. (D) is ungrammatical.
Key point: Did + subject + verb → Was/Were + subject + past participle.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
Are you familiar ________ the rules of chess?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) with
Why: A person is "familiar with" something he or she knows well.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not standard here. ("Familiar to" is used the other way round: "The face is familiar to me.")
Key point: I am familiar with it; it is familiar to me.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Wear your helmet; ________, the police may fine you.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) otherwise
Why: "Otherwise" means "if not": if you do not wear a helmet, you may be fined.
Why not the others: (B) adds a point. (C) gives a result. (D) shows contrast.
Key point: Otherwise = or else.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. the plastic waste
B. Last Sunday, a group of volunteers
C. around the lake
D. collected
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, D, A, C
Why: The opener with the subject (B) is followed by the verb (D), the object (A) and the place (C).
Why not the others: (A) and (C) start with a lower-case part. (D) puts the object before the verb.
Key point: Subject, verb, object, then place.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. This thread shows the words "Bharat" and "RBI" when held against the light.
B. Indian banknotes carry several security features to prevent forgery.
C. Another feature is the watermark of Mahatma Gandhi beside the portrait.
D. One of these is a security thread running through the note.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, D, A, C
Why: B introduces "several security features"; D names "One of these"; A explains "This thread"; C adds "Another feature".
Why not the others: (A) and (D) separate "This thread" from the sentence that introduces it. (C) begins with "One of these" before the features are mentioned.
Key point: "One of these", "This thread" and "Another" link the sentences.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. has been chosen to sing
B. The girl who lives next door
C. at the Republic Day function
D. the national anthem
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) B, A, D, C
Why: "The girl who lives next door (B) has been chosen to sing (A) the national anthem (D) at the Republic Day function (C)." "Sing" needs its object straight after it.
Why not the others: (B) puts the object before the verb. (C) starts with a lower-case part. (D) leaves the subject without a verb until the end.
Key point: A verb is followed by its object.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
The thief was APPREHENDED at the railway station within an hour.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Arrested
Why: To apprehend a criminal is to arrest or seize him.
Why not the others: (A) is the opposite. (B) and (C) can happen without an arrest.
Key point: Apprehend can also mean to understand or to fear; context decides.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Altruist
(B) Sceptic
(C) Glutton
(D) Nomad

List-II
(I) A person who eats far too much
(II) A person who moves from place to place with no fixed home
(III) A person who doubts what others accept as true
(IV) A person who cares unselfishly for the welfare of others
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Altruist — unselfish helper of others (IV); sceptic — a doubter (III); glutton — one who overeats (I); nomad — a wanderer with no fixed home (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps altruist and sceptic; (B) swaps sceptic and glutton; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: "Alter" means other: an altruist lives for others.

questions.sub_topic: Living on land and in water
questions.question: Choose the one word for: "An animal that can live both on land and in water"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Amphibian
Why: An amphibian (Greek "amphi", both + "bios", life), such as a frog, lives both on land and in water.
Why not the others: (B) feeds its young on milk. (C) is a cold-blooded animal with scales. (D) means living only in water.
Key point: "Amphi-" means both, as in amphitheatre (seats on both sides).

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to LENIENT:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Strict
Why: Lenient means mild and tolerant in punishing or judging; strict means demanding obedience to rules.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are close in meaning. (D) is unrelated.
Key point: A lenient teacher forgives late homework; a strict one does not.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to ADVERSITY:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Hardship
Why: Adversity means a difficult or unpleasant situation; hardship has the same meaning.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) only look similar. (D) is the opposite.
Key point: True friends stand by us in adversity.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "The guide warned us"
A. go into the forest
B. that it was dangerous
C. after sunset
D. to
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B, D, A, C
Why: "The guide warned us that it was dangerous (B) to (D) go into the forest (A) after sunset (C)." "Dangerous" is followed by "to + verb".
Why not the others: (A) begins with "to go" and leaves the "that" clause stranded. (B) gives "dangerous go into the forest to". (D) begins with a bare verb.
Key point: It is + adjective + to + verb.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
After the long trek, the boys were ________ and ate everything on the table.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ravenous
Why: "Ravenous" means extremely hungry.
Why not the others: (A) means having had enough. (B) and (D) do not explain eating everything.
Key point: The action (ate everything) decides the word.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The ________ farmers rebuilt their homes within months of the flood.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) resilient
Why: "Resilient" means able to recover quickly from difficulties.
Why not the others: (B) means easily broken. (C) means unwilling. (D) means in low spirits, which contradicts rebuilding quickly.
Key point: The result ("rebuilt ... within months") shows resilience.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. such a large crowd
B. had the village seen
C. Never before
D. at a wedding
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C, B, A, D
Why: "Never before (C) had the village seen (B) such a large crowd (A) at a wedding (D)." After "Never before", the auxiliary comes before the subject.
Why not the others: (A) puts the object before the verb. (B) starts with a lower-case part. (C) separates the negative opener from the inverted verb.
Key point: Never/Seldom/Rarely + auxiliary + subject.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
She said to me, "Please help me with this box."
options: A) She told me that please help her with that box.
B) She said me to help her with this box.
C) She requested me to help her with that box.
D) She ordered me to help me with that box.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) She requested me to help her with that box.
Why: A polite request with "please" is reported with "requested" + object + "to" + verb; "me" becomes "her" and "this" becomes "that".
Why not the others: (A) keeps "please" in a "that" clause. (B) "said me" is wrong, and "this" is not changed. (D) changes a request into an order and gets the pronoun wrong.
Key point: Please → requested ... to.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: police, any other, neither nor, since
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. The police have arrested the thief.
B. Gold is more precious than any metal.
C. Neither he nor I am to blame.
D. He has been ill since three days.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A and C only
Why: A is correct: "police" takes a plural verb. In C, the verb agrees with the nearer subject "I" ("am").
Why not the others: B should be "than any other metal" (gold is itself a metal). D should be "for three days" ("since" is used with a point in time). Options (A), (C) and (D) include B or D.
Key point: For + a period; since + a point in time.

questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Metaphor
(B) Oxymoron
(C) Pun
(D) Personification

List-II
(I) The old car coughed and groaned up the hill.
(II) The classroom was a zoo when the teacher left.
(III) Seasoned cooks are always well-seasoned.
(IV) The guide spoke in an open secret about the treasure.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: The classroom is called a zoo — metaphor (II); "open secret" joins opposites — oxymoron (IV); "seasoned" means experienced and also flavoured — pun (III); a car that coughs and groans — personification (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps metaphor and oxymoron; (C) swaps oxymoron and pun; (D) swaps pun and personification.
Key point: A pun plays on two meanings of one word.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
It is ________ to swim in the river during the monsoon.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) dangerous
Why: After "It is", an adjective is needed: "It is dangerous to swim".
Why not the others: (B) is a noun. (C) is an adverb. (D) is a verb.
Key point: It is + adjective + to + verb.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
You can always rely ________ her to finish the work on time.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) on
Why: The verb "rely" takes "on" (or "upon").
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not used with "rely".
Key point: Rely on, count on, depend on.

questions.question:
Select the words that mean "easily broken":
A. fragile
B. agile
C. brittle
D. docile
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
D) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A and C only
Why: "Fragile" and "brittle" both mean easily broken or damaged.
Why not the others: B (agile) means able to move quickly and easily. D (docile) means quiet and easy to control. Options (A), (B) and (D) include one of them.
Key point: Fragile and agile rhyme but differ in meaning.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
The new classrooms are bright and SPACIOUS.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cramped
Why: Spacious means having plenty of room; cramped means uncomfortably small.
Why not the others: (A) is a synonym. (C) and (D) are unrelated.
Key point: Spacious comes from "space".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
If you ________ a real effort, you can improve your handwriting in a month.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) make
Why: The fixed collocation is "make an effort".
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) do not go with "effort".
Key point: Make an effort, make a mistake, make a decision.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
You can go to the concert ________ you finish your homework first.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) provided that
Why: "Provided that" means "on the condition that".
Why not the others: (A) means "if not" and reverses the sense. (B) means "whether or not". (D) must be followed by a noun.
Key point: Provided (that) = only if.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

For thousands of years, millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were everyday food in much of India. They are small-seeded grains that grow well where other crops struggle. Millets need far less water than rice, tolerate heat and poor soil, and many varieties are ready for harvest in just a few months. A farmer in a dry district can often raise a millet crop on rain alone.

From the 1960s, however, the Green Revolution brought high-yielding varieties of rice and wheat, along with irrigation, fertilisers and government support for buying these two grains. Farmers naturally grew what paid best, and the area under millets fell sharply. In many cities, millets came to be seen as "poor people's food", while polished white rice and wheat flour became symbols of a better life.

Nutrition scientists now see millets very differently. Most millets are rich in fibre and minerals. Ragi is one of the best plant sources of calcium, and bajra is a good source of iron. Millets contain no gluten, and because they are digested slowly, they release sugar into the blood more gradually than polished rice does, which can help people who need to control their blood sugar.

In 2023, which the United Nations declared the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion, these grains returned to the spotlight. Millet dosas, biscuits and noodles appeared on shop shelves, and several states added millets to school meals. With rainfall becoming less predictable, supporters argue that these hardy grains are not a step backwards but a sensible choice for the future, good for the farmer, for the consumer and for the land.

Question: According to the passage, which year did the United Nations declare the International Year of Millets?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2023
Why: "In 2023, which the United Nations declared the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion, these grains returned to the spotlight."
Why not the others: (A) is near the start of the Green Revolution. (B) and (C) are not mentioned.
Key point: Detail questions are answered from the exact line.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In 2023, which the United Nations declared the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion, these grains returned to the spotlight. With rainfall becoming less predictable, supporters argue that these hardy grains are not a step backwards but a sensible choice for the future, good for the farmer, for the consumer and for the land.

Question: Why, according to the passage, did the area under millets fall after the 1960s?
options: A) Millets stopped growing because the rainfall had increased
B) Rice and wheat received support and paid farmers better
C) Scientists proved that millets were poor in nutrition
D) The government banned millets from being sold in cities
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Rice and wheat received support and paid farmers better
Why: The Green Revolution brought high-yielding rice and wheat with "government support for buying these two grains. Farmers naturally grew what paid best."
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are not stated. (C) Scientists now praise millets' nutrition.
Key point: "Naturally" points to a cause the writer thinks is obvious.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In 2023, which the United Nations declared the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion, these grains returned to the spotlight. With rainfall becoming less predictable, supporters argue that these hardy grains are not a step backwards but a sensible choice for the future, good for the farmer, for the consumer and for the land.

Question: In the last paragraph, millets are called "hardy grains". Here "hardy" means:
options: A) Able to survive difficult conditions
B) Very hard to cook and chew
C) Difficult to find in the market
D) Grown only by brave farmers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Able to survive difficult conditions
Why: The passage has shown that millets tolerate heat, poor soil and little water; with less predictable rainfall, these hardy grains can still be grown.
Why not the others: (B) confuses "hardy" with "hard". (C) and (D) are not suggested.
Key point: Use earlier details to decide the meaning of a word.

questions.sub_topic: Statement the passage does not support

Question: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
options: A) Ragi is a good plant source of calcium
B) Millets release sugar into the blood more slowly than polished rice
C) Millets need more irrigation than wheat does
D) Some states have added millets to school meals
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Millets need more irrigation than wheat does
Why: The passage says millets "need far less water than rice" and can be raised "on rain alone". Saying they need more irrigation than wheat contradicts this.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are all stated.
Key point: A statement can fail by contradicting the passage, not only by being absent from it.

questions.sub_topic: The writer's purpose in the millet passage
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

For thousands of years, millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were everyday food in much of India. They are small-seeded grains that grow well where other crops struggle. Millets need far less water than rice, tolerate heat and poor soil, and many varieties are ready for harvest in just a few months. A farmer in a dry district can often raise a millet crop on rain alone.

From the 1960s, however, the Green Revolution brought high-yielding varieties of rice and wheat, along with irrigation, fertilisers and government support for buying these two grains. Farmers naturally grew what paid best, and the area under millets fell sharply. In many cities, millets came to be seen as "poor people's food", while polished white rice and wheat flour became symbols of a better life.

Nutrition scientists now see millets very differently. Most millets are rich in fibre and minerals. Ragi is one of the best plant sources of calcium, and bajra is a good source of iron. Millets contain no gluten, and because they are digested slowly, they release sugar into the blood more gradually than polished rice does, which can help people who need to control their blood sugar.

In 2023, which the United Nations declared the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion, these grains returned to the spotlight. Millet dosas, biscuits and noodles appeared on shop shelves, and several states added millets to school meals. With rainfall becoming less predictable, supporters argue that these hardy grains are not a step backwards but a sensible choice for the future, good for the farmer, for the consumer and for the land.

Question: What does the writer mainly set out to do in the passage?
options: A) To blame farmers for giving up traditional grains
B) To give recipes for millet dosas and biscuits
C) To argue that the Green Revolution was a failure
D) To show why millets are being valued again
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) To show why millets are being valued again
Why: The passage traces millets' decline and explains, through nutrition and climate, why they are returning.
Why not the others: (A) The writer says farmers "naturally" chose what paid best. (B) Recipes are not given. (C) The Green Revolution is described, not condemned.
Key point: Purpose covers the whole passage, especially its ending.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

For three months Raju did not touch the wheel. He swept the yard, carried water, kneaded clay with his feet until his legs ached, and watched Ustad Karim's hands. The old potter rarely spoke. When he did, it was usually to say, "Not yet."

Then one morning in March, Ustad Karim stood up from the wheel and pointed at the stool. Raju sat down, his heart thumping. He threw a lump of wet clay on to the centre, set the wheel spinning and pressed with both hands, as he had seen his master do a thousand times.

The clay wobbled, leaned and flew off the wheel into the dust.

He tried again. This time the walls rose a little, then folded in on themselves like a tired flower. The third pot collapsed. The fourth tore. By noon his hands were raw, his shirt was grey with clay, and the boys from the next street had gathered at the gate to laugh.

Ustad Karim said nothing. He only brought another lump of clay and set it on the wheel.

It was late afternoon when Raju lifted his hands from the ninth pot and found that it was still standing. It leaned a little to the left, and its rim was thicker on one side than the other. He looked at it and felt like crying.

The next day, when the kiln was opened, Ustad Karim took out the crooked little pot, filled it with water from the well and set it beside his own sleeping-mat. "Every potter's first pot is ugly," he said. "Mine was uglier." It was the longest speech Raju had ever heard him make.

Question: What did Raju do during his first three months with Ustad Karim?
options: A) He did the yard work and watched his master
B) He made small pots for the market
C) He sold his master's pots in the next street
D) He fired pots in the kiln each evening
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) He did the yard work and watched his master
Why: "He swept the yard, carried water, kneaded clay with his feet ... and watched Ustad Karim's hands."
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not stated; he did not touch the wheel.
Key point: Answer from the details listed in the passage.

Question: Ustad Karim usually said, "Not yet." What does this suggest about his teaching?
options: A) He did not want Raju to become a potter at all
B) He was too busy to answer Raju's questions
C) He believed a learner must wait until ready
D) He thought Raju was too old to learn
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) He believed a learner must wait until ready
Why: He keeps Raju watching and doing basic work for three months before letting him sit at the wheel; "Not yet" means the time has not come.
Why not the others: (A) He later lets Raju try. (B) and (D) are not suggested.
Key point: Repeated words reveal a character's way of thinking.

Question: "The walls rose a little, then folded in on themselves like a tired flower." This comparison shows that the pot:
options: A) Was painted with patterns of flowers
C) Grew taller than the earlier pots
D) Broke into sharp pieces at once
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Drooped and collapsed slowly
Why: A tired flower droops and bends; the soft clay walls sank inwards in the same way.
Why not the others: (A) takes "flower" literally. (C) and (D) contradict the description.
Key point: Ask what the thing compared has in common with the comparison.

Question: After each failure, Ustad Karim "said nothing. He only brought another lump of clay". This shows that he:
options: A) Was angry with Raju and refused to speak to him
B) Wanted the boys at the gate to go away
C) Thought that Raju would never succeed
D) Quietly encouraged Raju to keep trying
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Quietly encouraged Raju to keep trying
Why: By silently giving him more clay, the master tells Raju to try again rather than give up.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are contradicted by his later kindness. (B) is not suggested.
Key point: Actions can speak where a character is silent.

Question: Why does Ustad Karim keep Raju's crooked pot beside his sleeping-mat?
options: A) To honour the effort of a first success, which every potter makes
B) Because it is the best pot that came out of the kiln
C) Because he wants Raju to sell it to the boys at the gate
D) To remind himself to stop teaching apprentices
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) To honour the effort of a first success, which every potter makes
Why: He says, "Every potter's first pot is ugly ... Mine was uglier," and uses it himself, showing respect for Raju's first real achievement.
Why not the others: (B) It is crooked and uneven. (C) and (D) are not suggested.
Key point: A small act may show a character's deepest feeling.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A Letter Home from the Hills

Dear Amma, the hills are bigger than you said,
and greener, and the clouds walk in the street;
they come into our classroom without knocking
and sit, like sleepy cows, about our feet.

The food is fine. The porridge could be warmer.
I share my room with boys from five states;
one snores like a tractor climbing a mountain,
one cries at night, and nobody says he hates

this place, though every Sunday after letters
the dormitory is very quiet and still.
I am learning to tie my own tie properly,
and to climb, without stopping, Chapel Hill.

Last week I saw a flame-red pheasant
cross the path as if it owned the wood;
I wished that you could see it. Do not worry.
I wear the sweater. I am being good.

Tell Baba that I came third in the maths test.
Tell Meenu she may keep my old cricket bat.
And Amma — if the mango tree is fruiting,
save one for me. Just one. I'll come back for that.

Question: "The clouds walk in the street; / they come into our classroom without knocking." The main figure of speech is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Personification
Why: The clouds walk and enter without knocking, as people would — personification. (The hill school is so high that clouds drift through it.)
Why not the others: (A) It describes something real in the hills, not an exaggeration. (B) The clouds are not called something else here. (D) No sound is imitated.
Key point: Human actions given to nature signal personification.

Question: "Nobody says he hates / this place, though every Sunday after letters / the dormitory is very quiet and still." What do these lines suggest?
options: A) The boys miss home, though none of them admits it
B) The boys are punished if they talk on Sundays
C) The boys are busy writing answers to their letters
D) The dormitory is empty because everyone goes home
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The boys miss home, though none of them admits it
Why: Letters from home leave the boys silent and thoughtful; the speaker hints at homesickness that nobody says aloud.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are not suggested. (D) The boys are there; it is quiet, not empty.
Key point: Poems often suggest a feeling instead of naming it.

Question: In the fourth stanza, the speaker writes, "Do not worry. / I wear the sweater. I am being good." Why does he add these lines?
options: A) He is boasting about his new sweater
B) He wants to reassure his mother
C) He has been told to write them by a teacher
D) He wants his mother to send a new sweater
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) He wants to reassure his mother
Why: After wishing his mother could see the pheasant, he comforts her, answering the worries a mother would have.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not suggested by the tone.
Key point: Short, simple sentences can carry strong feeling.

Question: In the last stanza, the speaker asks his mother to "save one for me. Just one." What does this request show?
options: A) He does not like mangoes very much
B) He thinks his family is too poor to buy mangoes
C) He wants to sell the mango at school
D) He longs for home and its small, familiar things
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) He longs for home and its small, familiar things
Why: The mango tree stands for home; asking for "just one" shows how much the small things of home mean to him, and that he plans to return.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not suggested.
Key point: Endings often carry the poem's central feeling.
